query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Optimized, controlled mild oxidative pretreatment of inert gas condensed, near‐equiatomic MnFeCoNiCu nanoparticles promotes the formation of a uniform, ultrathin, self-limiting oxide passivation layer that effectively suppresses elemental segregation and sintering during high-temperature operation.
generation.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic MnFeCoNiCu solid-solution nanoparticles prepared via inert gas condensation, ensuring minimal initial elemental segregation.
generation.intervention: Implement an optimized mild oxidation pretreatment by carefully tuning oxygen pressure, temperature, and duration to produce a uniform, defect-minimized ultrathin oxide layer prior to thermal cycling. This is compared to a baseline set maintained under strictly reducing conditions.
generation.conditions: Subject both oxidized and reducing-condition nanoparticles to cyclic thermal treatments under service-relevant atmospheres: for catalytic evaluation at 773–1173 K under alternate mildly oxidizing and reducing conditions, and for thermoelectric testing from 473–1923 K.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a stable, uniform, ultrathin oxide passivation layer (rich in oxidation-prone elements such as Mn and Cu) that limits surface diffusion and elemental segregation during high-temperature cycling.
generation.mechanism: Under operational conditions, differential oxide formation energies drive surface segregation and elemental mobility. Optimized mild oxidation induces a controlled formation of a passivating oxide that pins the surface composition, preventing further diffusion, sintering, and phase decomposition. This passivation mitigates the enthalpic driving force for elemental segregation by stabilizing the nanoparticle’s high configurational entropy state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles receiving the optimized oxidative pretreatment will maintain a more stable single-phase solid solution with reduced elemental segregation, as confirmed by in situ XRD, TEM, and XPS after extended thermal cycling. This improved structural integrity will correlate with better preserved catalytic activity (turnover frequency, selectivity) and thermoelectric performance compared with baseline nanoparticles kept under reducing conditions.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized under inert (reducing) conditions, which do not develop an effective oxide passivation layer and are expected to exhibit greater elemental segregation and phase instability under the same harsh service regimes.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to near-equiatomic MnFeCoNiCu nanoparticles produced via inert gas condensation and tested under specified thermal regime conditions (773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectrics). Variations in synthesis method or significant deviations from the optimized oxidation parameters may affect passivation efficacy.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty regarding the precise sensitivity of nanoparticle stability to slight variations in oxidation pretreatment parameters; nonuniformity or defects in the oxide layer could lead to localized degradation. Further optimization and careful characterization are required to delineate the window in which passivation is maximally effective.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of near-equiatomic MnFeCoNiCu nanoparticles: one undergoing the optimized mild oxidation pretreatment and one maintained under reducing conditions. Subject both sets to identical cyclic thermal treatments under service-relevant atmospheres (773–1173 K for catalytic cycling and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric cycling). Thoroughly characterize the oxide layer uniformity, thickness, and structural integrity using in situ XRD, TEM, and XPS both before and after thermal cycling.
measurements: In situ and ex situ XRD for phase stability and detection of secondary phases
TEM for microstructural and oxide layer uniformity analysis
XPS for assessing surface composition and oxidation states
Catalytic performance metrics (e.g., turnover frequency, selectivity) and thermoelectric property measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized oxidation pretreatment does not lead to a statistically significant improvement in the structural stability (reduced elemental segregation and absence of secondary phase formation) and operational performance (consistent catalytic and thermoelectric properties) compared to the baseline reducing-condition nanoparticles, the hypothesis that the protective oxide layer governs nanoparticle stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 2 shows a CoCrFeNiMn alloy constituting a single-phase FCC structure that is oxidized at 400 °C for 120 min. A relatively lower temperature compared to past studies is chosen for this study to suppress the phase transformation tendency in this super-saturated alloy. The thin oxide film (~20 nm) forms a compositionally layered structure. Starting from the equiatomic base alloy, a Ni-enriched layer is followed by Cr-rich oxide followed by Fe, Mn, and Co-rich oxide layers (Fig. 1g). The enrichment of elements in the top layer, however, is not uniform. While the Mn layer appears on the top, at certain locations, bubble-like Fe pockets can be seen on the top layer of the surface (Fig. 2b). Furthermore, due to the solid-state nature of the oxidation, atomic diffusion from the bulk alloy results in the formation of defects within inner layers (Fig. 2c). Unlike liquids, solid surfaces undergo elastic deformation as atoms diffuse through to form the oxide layer. We infer that Al addition does not have significant electronic interaction with Co and Ni (Fig. 4h, i), this is shown as their oxidation behavior remains the same in Fig. 4d. Figure 4j summarizes these interactions where Mn-Al tends to have the strongest interaction and both Ni and Co being the weakest. This study uncovers the oxidation process in compositionally complex alloys. Our study involved subjecting an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy to oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar oxygen pressure for both ex situ and in situ observations. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide). We chose a relatively low oxidation temperature to prevent phase transformation in the alloy, focusing solely on examining the oxidation process in the super-saturated alloy condition. proposals.material_system: Near‐equiatomic MnFeCoNiCu solid-solution nanoparticles (prepared via inert gas condensation to ensure minimal initial segregation)
proposals.intervention: Introduce a controlled, mild oxidative pretreatment that promotes the formation of ultrathin, uniform oxide passivation layers on the nanoparticle surfaces, versus a baseline set maintained under strictly reducing conditions.
proposals.conditions: Subject both sets of nanoparticles to cyclic thermal treatments in relevant atmospheres: for catalytic tests at 773–1173 K in a mildly oxidizing/reducing cycling environment and for thermoelectric evaluation between 473–1923 K.
proposals.structural_mediator: The formation (or absence) of a stable, self-limiting passivation oxide layer at the nanoparticle surface that mitigates further elemental segregation and prevents coarsening.
proposals.mechanism: Under service conditions, differences in the intrinsic oxide formation energies among Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, and Cu drive surface segregation. The controlled mild oxidation is hypothesized to allow preferential formation of a protective ultrathin oxide (likely enriched in the more oxidation-prone elements such as Mn and Cu) that pins the solid-solution structure in place. This passivation layer thus counteracts the enthalpic driving forces for elemental diffusion and sintering while preserving the high configurational entropy that stabilizes the single-phase state.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the reducing-baseline nanoparticles, the pre-oxidized nanoparticles will exhibit a more stable phase structure—with significantly less evidence of elemental segregation or phase decomposition—as assessed by in situ XRD, TEM, and XPS after extended high-temperature cycling. This should correlate with a maintained or even improved catalytic performance (e.g., turnover frequency and selectivity) and thermoelectric properties over prolonged service exposure.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach directly tests whether the ability to form a controlled, self-limiting oxide passivation layer governs the structural and chemical stability of multi-element HEA nanoparticles under harsh operating temperatures. By controlling the oxidation state at the surface, the experiment distinguishes between entropy-driven stabilization and the competing chemical segregation/oxidation mechanisms, providing a clear falsification test: if pre-oxidation does not yield enhanced stability (i.e., if both sample sets degrade similarly), then the role of surface passivation in stability is disproven.

critiques.addresses_problem: The direction directly addresses the open question by testing whether the formation of a controlled oxide passivation layer governs the structural and chemical stability of near‐equiatomic MnFeCoNiCu nanoparticles under high-temperature service conditions. It clearly focuses on the mechanism behind segregation and stability.
critiques.constraints: The proposed intervention respects the material system (MnFeCoNiCu nanoparticles), the thermal regimes for catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) applications, and the requirement for maintaining low noble-metal content. The experimental conditions and controlled pretreatment are consistent with the stated constraints.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanistic hypothesis is physically sound: it leverages differences in oxide formation energies to create an ultrathin, self-limiting passivation layer that can suppress further elemental diffusion and sintering. However, there is a risk that the oxidation process may lead to non-uniform oxide layers or defect formation (as observed in related studies, e.g., PMC11169556) rather than the ideal protective film.
critiques.feasibility: The approach is feasible with established methods (inert gas condensation, controlled mild oxidation, in situ XRD/TEM/XPS analysis) and builds upon existing work on layered oxides in similar HEA systems.
critiques.evidence: The candidate direction is supported by multiple pieces of evidence that report layered oxide formation and selective elemental oxidation in similar systems (e.g., PMC11169556 :: web::008 and PMC11169556 :: web::018 discuss controlled oxidation and layered oxide structures, and other records confirm that selective oxidation can influence structural stability).
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the controlled mild oxidation may not yield a uniformly protective, defect‐free passivation layer. Instead, the oxidation process could produce non-uniform films with localized defects or compositional inhomogeneities, which may still allow elemental segregation or even impair catalytic performance.
critiques.fix: Refine the oxidation pretreatment conditions — for example, by optimizing temperature, oxygen pressure, and duration — to ensure a more uniform, defect-minimized oxide layer formation, and include in-depth characterization of the oxide’s uniformity and thickness before high-temperature testing.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly addresses the central question by targeting the mechanism of protective oxide passivation layers in near‐equiatomic MnFeCoNiCu nanoparticles under high-temperature service conditions. The proposed intervention (controlled mild oxidation) is well-founded by prior evidence showing layered oxide formation, and its potential to suppress elemental segregation, which is key to maintaining stability. The critic’s suggestion to refine and optimize the oxidation pretreatment conditions to ensure uniform and defect‐minimized oxide layers is both practical and necessary. By adopting this direction with fine-tuning to the oxidation parameters, the study can clearly distinguish the role of oxide passivation in structural stability versus competing segregation mechanisms.
